Repo: /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim. The compiled driver is at build/andes-sim and all vsim engines are built. A python venv with nbconvert is at /tmp/nbenv (kernel name "nbenv", inherits system matplotlib).

YOUR JOB: execute the notebook `docs/andes_sim_memory_tutorial.ipynb` end-to-end against the live build and report exactly which cells work and which fail. Do NOT edit the original notebook.

How to execute (run from repo root, capture ALL failures in one pass with --allow-errors):
  cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
  out=/tmp/nbout_$(basename docs/andes_sim_memory_tutorial.ipynb .ipynb).ipynb
  timeout 580 /tmp/nbenv/bin/jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --allow-errors \
    --ExecutePreprocessor.kernel_name=nbenv --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=420 \
    --output "$out" docs/andes_sim_memory_tutorial.ipynb 2>&1 | tail -15

Then inspect the executed output notebook ($out) for cells whose outputs contain an error (output_type == "error"); for each, record the cell index, ename, evalue, and the first ~3 lines of that cell's source. Use python to parse the json (e.g. /tmp/nbenv/bin/python).

Notes / cautions:
- Some cells shell out to ./andes-sim or build/andes-sim and run cycle-accurate vsim - these are slow but should finish in minutes for the small fixtures used in tutorials. This host has 128 cores; if a single cell itself spawns the parallel e2e harness, that can saturate CPU - if you see such a cell, note it but it should still complete.
- If the whole nbconvert run hits the 580s timeout, report executed=false-ish (health=partial/fail) and identify the cell index it was stuck on (the last cell with no output in $out).
- A cell that intentionally demonstrates an error/limitation (the limitations notebook may do this) is NOT a failure if its output is the expected demonstrated message - judge by whether the cell's behavior matches the surrounding markdown's intent. Flag ambiguous ones in issues.
- Count total_cells and code_cells. Set health: pass (all code cells ran clean), partial (some failed but most work), fail (most/all fail or not executable), not-executable (missing kernel/deps unrelated to the notebook's own logic).
Return ONLY the structured object.

--- [MD CELL 0] ---
# andes-sim tutorial: guest memory (`--mem-size`)

Every model defaults to a small guest memory (128 MiB). This tutorial
shows how to request more with one flag, what each model does with it,
and where the bytes actually live.

You will:

1. build a program that needs 2 GiB of guest memory,
2. watch it fault under the default, then fix it with `--mem-size`,
3. learn the 2 GiB cap (the AE350 DRAM window) and how each model
   reports it,
4. see the hybrid model's backing-store tiers (`/dev/shm`, then
   `~/.cache/andes-sim`) and how to pin one,
5. check your machine with `andes-sim doctor`.

--- [MD CELL 2] ---
## 1. A program that needs 2 GiB

The program writes a pattern at `0x7FFFF000` - 4 KiB below the top of
the 2 GiB DRAM window - and verifies it twice: once immediately, and
once inside the ROI markers (on a hybrid run that second check executes
on the RTL engine, after the handoff).

It links against the vplat runtime, so the same binary runs on every
model, and a `printf` inside the ROI is allowed (it bottoms out in a
UART both engines model):

--- [MD CELL 4] ---
## 2. The default is small - watch it fault

`--model fast` is QEMU as-is: andes-sim does not inject any memory
setting, so QEMU's own 128 MiB default applies. A load at 2 GiB has no
memory behind it, and the runtime's trap handler reports a load access
fault (`Exception code: 5`) at exactly our address (`mtval:
0x7ffff000`):

--- [MD CELL 6] ---
Request the memory and the same binary passes. On `fast` the flag
just forwards a plain `-m 2048M` to QEMU - nothing else changes (and a
`-m` you pass yourself after `--` would still win):

--- [MD CELL 8] ---
## 3. The cap: 2 GiB

The AE350 SoC decodes DRAM at `0x0 .. 0x80000000`, so 2 GiB is a hard
ceiling for any QEMU-backed model. Each model reports an over-ask in
its own way - `fast` lets QEMU say it:

--- [MD CELL 10] ---
...while `hybrid` rejects it in the driver, **before** allocating
the (potentially huge) backing file - note there is no `[hsim mmap]`
line:

--- [MD CELL 12] ---
(`--model cycle` has nothing to size - the RTL engine always
models its full DRAM window - so there `--mem-size` is validated and
declared a no-op on stderr.)

## 4. hybrid: one flag, three views of the same bytes

On a hybrid run `--mem-size` sizes one shared thing: a sparse file that
is at once

- the **mmap** both legs share,
- QEMU's **memory backend** (= guest RAM), and
- the RTL engine's **RAM window** after the handoff.

The `[hsim mmap]` status line shows where it lives. The file is sparse:
2 GiB of address space, but only pages the program touches cost RAM -
this run really uses a few MiB:

--- [MD CELL 14] ---
Both checks pass: the pattern QEMU wrote at 2 GiB - 4 KiB is read
back by the RTL engine through the shared mmap, and the
`[marker window_cycles]` line prices the ROI on the real core.

### Where the file lives: backing tiers

The backing directory comes from a two-tier list, first fit wins
(fit = size + 256 MiB free):

1. `/dev/shm` - tmpfs, RAM speed;
2. `~/.cache/andes-sim` - disk-backed, for when the request exceeds
   tmpfs (hot pages still sit in the page cache, so the cost is
   background writeback only).

A fallback is never silent - the status line carries the reason, e.g.

    [hsim mmap] 2.0 GiB at /home/u/.cache/andes-sim (free: 2.1 TiB) (fallback: /dev/shm too small (1.2 GiB free))

`HSIM_MMAP_DIR` pins a single directory instead (no fallback past the
pin - too small is then a hard error):

--- [MD CELL 16] ---
## 5. Check your machine

`andes-sim doctor` ends with an `mmap tiers:` section: each tier with
its free space. On WSL2 it also warns when the repo or a tier directory
sits under `/mnt/` (drvfs - slow, and `MAP_SHARED` is not coherent
there) and reminds you that `/dev/shm` is capped by the WSL VM memory
(`.wslconfig`, `memory=`):

--- [MD CELL 18] ---
## 6. Portability notes

The hybrid handoff needs both legs on **one Linux kernel**, with the
mmap on a filesystem local to that kernel:

| Host | How to run |
|------|-----------|
| Linux | native - everything in this tutorial as-is |
| Windows (WSL2) | as Linux; keep the repo and mmap dirs on ext4 (`~/...`), never `/mnt/c`; raise `memory=` in `.wslconfig` if tier 1 is small |
| macOS | run-only: `./andes-sim` re-execs inside a prebuilt Linux runtime image (podman machine VM); the mmap lives in the VM's `/dev/shm`. `brew install podman && podman machine init && podman machine start`, then use `./andes-sim` exactly as above. Knobs: `ANDES_SIM_IMAGE`, `ANDES_SIM_SHM_SIZE`. |

## Recap

| Model | `--mem-size SPEC` does | default | over 2G |
|-------|------------------------|---------|---------|
| `fast` | forwards a plain QEMU `-m` (only when given) | QEMU's own 128 MiB | QEMU's own error |
| `hybrid` | sizes the shared mmap = QEMU backend = RTL RAM window | 128 MiB | driver error, before allocating |
| `cycle` | validated, then a stderr note - the RTL always models its full window | full window | n/a |

Details: `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` section 2.5 (memory + tiers) and 2.5.1
(WSL2/macOS).
